query: Tungsten is considered for fusion first-wall and divertor service, but it has low strength, limited thermal-shock resistance, a high ductile-brittle transition temperature, and develops dislocation loops and He bubbles under energetic-particle exposure that increase hardening and brittleness; subsequent annealing does not fully remove the damage. Earlier efforts based on cold rolling, wire drawing, and severe plastic deformation sought to improve W, yet fracture resistance remains unresolved and nanocrystalline W still suffers severe damage. Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 showed better radiation resistance than nanocrystalline W and negligible hardening, but Cr-V-rich precipitates appeared at 8 dpa. W29Ta42Cr5V16Hf8 showed neither dislocation loops nor precipitates at 10 dpa, while its greater number of constituents complicates bulk fabrication; the low melting point of Cr also impairs fabrication feasibility in both compositions. For nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exposed to energetic particles near 8 dpa, what single intervention could suppress precipitate formation while preserving low hardening, radiation resistance, and practical bulk manufacturability? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predict measurable outcomes against the unmodified baseline, define dose and specimen-temperature limits, identify supporting observations from the prior work summarized above, and specify a controlled exposure and post-exposure characterization experiment whose results would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of Hf to the nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will suppress precipitate formation while preserving low hardening, radiation resistance, and practical bulk manufacturability.
generation.conditions: Exposure to energetic particles near 8 dpa
generation.structural_mediator: Configurational entropy of mixing in multicomponent alloys
generation.mechanism: Stabilization of the solid solution based on simple underlying face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structures
generation.predicted_outcome: Suppressed precipitate formation, low hardening, radiation resistance, and practical bulk manufacturability
generation.boundary: Dose limit: 8 dpa, Specimen-temperature limit: 1073 K
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Hf to be introduced is uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled exposure and post-exposure characterization experiment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If precipitate formation is not suppressed, or if hardening increases, or if radiation resistance decreases, then the hypothesis is falsified

In the slightly lower temperature ranging from 1250 to 1600 K, the formation of nanometer-scale bubbles is observed () in W exposed to the He plasma. At larger He ion fluences, close to International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) () working conditions, exposed surfaces are found to exhibit a nanostructured surface morphology (), termed as fuzz. The increased surface area and fragility of these nanostructured surfaces raise new concerns for the use of W as a fusion reactor PFM, particularly as a source of high-Z dust that will contaminate the plasma.
Strategies such as adding different alloying elements (e.g., W-Re and W-Ti) or nanostructure-engineered W are being investigated to improve the material processing and working properties. Related to the second strategy, recent work shows that state-of-the-art nanocrystalline W samples exhibit substantial formation of He bubbles at the grain boundaries, which leads to decohesion and poor mechanical properties at operational temperatures (), reducing its applicability in fusion environments. ## HEA morphology and thermal stability
A detailed characterization of the morphology and phase details of the as-deposited HEA films results in a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with size in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm) with an underlying single-phase BCC, with a lattice constant of ~3.2 Å (see the Supplementary Materials). Before irradiation, we performed EDS (Fig. 1) and APT (Fig. 2) to investigate the composition of this alloy. EDS line scan (Fig. 1A) was performed to determine the composition in the alloy (Fig. 1B), while EDS mapping (Fig. 1C) shows uniform elemental composition. o grain boundaries was also observed to be similar to as-deposited films. No evidence for disappearance of compositional striations or clustering of elements was observed in the APT results, indicating that compositional clustering was not homogenously distributed in the sample after heating. Not all grains demonstrated compositional clustering, indicating grain variations regarding elemental segregation.
## Irradiation
We then irradiated the HEA films in situ at the IVEM–Tandem Facility with 1-MeV Kr+2 and 1073 K, with a dpa rate of 0.0006 dpa s−1 to 1.6 dpa (fig. S4). During irradiation, no dislocation loops were observed. However, further and enhanced precipitation (black spot formation) was recognized. A higher dpa irradiation was then performed on a different film at the same temperature (1073 K) with a dpa rate of 0.0016 dpa s−1 to 8 dpa. The morphology during irradiation is shown in Fig. 3 (see also movies S1 and S2 for low and high doses, respectively). Precipitation was shown to occur during irradiation, where its intensity increased with dose. Notably, dislocation loops were not observed even at 8 dpa.
